title: Nearest Neighbors and Kernel Smoothing
description: Prediction by similarity: the k-nearest-neighbor rule, distance metrics, the curse of dimensionality and kernel regression.
overview: The simplest learning algorithm does no training. It stores the data, and to predict for a new point it looks up the most similar stored points and copies their labels. This is nearest-neighbor classification. Despite its simplicity it is a strong baseline, it has a clean theoretical guarantee, and it makes the dependence of learning on the geometry of the data easy to see.
The method also shows clearly what fails in high dimensions: when there are many features, no points are close to each other, and local methods starve for data.
objectives: Apply the k-nearest-neighbor rule for classification and regression, and see how k controls bias and variance.
Choose and scale a distance metric appropriately.
State the Cover–Hart bound relating 1-NN error to the Bayes error.
Explain the curse of dimensionality quantitatively.
Compute a kernel-weighted (Nadaraya–Watson) estimate and describe how nearest-neighbor search is accelerated.

sections.title: The k-nearest-neighbor rule
body: Given a query x, find the k training points closest to it under a distance d, the neighbors N_k(x). Then:

list: **Classification**: predict the most common label among the neighbors (a majority vote).
**Regression**: predict the average of the neighbors' labels, ŷ = (1/k) Σ_{i ∈ N_k(x)} y^{(i)}.
**Weighted** versions give closer neighbors more weight, for example w_i ∝ 1/d(x, x^{(i)}).

body: This is **instance-based** or **lazy** learning: there is no training phase and no parameters, but the whole data set must be stored and each prediction scans it. For k = 1 the decision regions are the cells of the **Voronoi diagram** of the training points: each cell is the set of points closer to one training point than to any other. The boundary between classes is piecewise linear and can be very irregular.

example.title: The prediction depends on k
example.problem: Training points: red at (1, 1), (2, 1), (3, 2) and blue at (4, 4), (5, 3). Classify the query (3, 3) with k = 1, 3 and 5 using Euclidean distance.

eq: k = 5: three red, two blue → red

solution: The prediction flips with k. A small k follows individual points (low bias, high variance), and a large k averages over a wide region.

body: k is the hyperparameter that sets the complexity. With k = 1 the training error is zero (each point is its own nearest neighbor) and the model is highly variable. As k grows the boundary smooths; at k = m the prediction is the global majority. Choose k by cross-validation, typically an odd number to avoid ties in two-class problems.

sections.title: Distance and similarity
body: The method is only as good as its notion of similarity. Common distances between x and z:

eqs: Manhattan distance; less sensitive to a single large difference
cosine similarity; compares direction and ignores length, common for text
Mahalanobis distance; accounts for scale and correlation of the features

body.warn: Features on larger scales dominate the distance. If income is in dollars (up to 10⁵) and age in years (up to 100), income alone decides who is near. Standardize every feature, or learn a metric, before using nearest neighbors. Irrelevant features add noise to every distance, so select features carefully.

body: Categorical features need a different measure, such as the Hamming distance (count of mismatches). For complex objects, a learned embedding (from a neural network) often supplies a distance in which Euclidean or cosine similarity works well. This is how modern image search and retrieval systems work.

check.q: Two documents are far apart in Euclidean distance only because one is much longer. Which measure ignores length?
wrong: Manhattan distance
Euclidean distance
Hamming distance

sections.title: How good can it be? The Cover–Hart bound
body: The Bayes error R* is the lowest error any classifier can achieve (see Generative Classifiers). For two classes, Cover and Hart (1967) showed that as the number of training points m → ∞ the error of the 1-nearest-neighbor rule satisfies

Without any model assumptions, the simplest rule is never more than twice as bad as the best possible classifier. The intuition: as m grows the nearest neighbor of x becomes arbitrarily close to x, so its label is a draw from the same conditional distribution P(y | x). It errs when the neighbor's label differs from the query's, with probability 2p(1 − p), where p = P(y = 1 | x), compared with the Bayes rule's min(p, 1 − p). A concrete case: at a spot where 90% of points are class 1 (p = 0.9), the best rule always says class 1 and errs 10% of the time. The 1-NN rule copies a random neighbor's label. It errs when query and neighbor disagree: query 1 and neighbor 0 (0.9 × 0.1) or query 0 and neighbor 1 (0.1 × 0.9), for a total of 0.18. That is under twice the Bayes error.

example.title: The bound in numbers
example.problem: If the Bayes error is 10%, what are the possible asymptotic errors of 1-NN? What if the Bayes error is 25%?
example.solution: For R* = 0.10: 2(0.1)(0.9) = 0.18, so 1-NN has error between 10% and 18%. For R* = 0.25: 2(0.25)(0.75) = 0.375, so the error is between 25% and 37.5%.

body: With k growing slowly with m (k → ∞ and k/m → 0) the k-NN rule is **consistent**: its error converges to the Bayes error for every distribution. Few methods have this property. The catch is that convergence can need an astronomical number of points when n is large, as the next section shows.

sections.title: The curse of dimensionality
body: Intuition built in two and three dimensions fails in high dimensions. Local methods assume that points exist near the query, and that assumption breaks down.

Suppose data are uniform in the unit cube [0, 1]ⁿ. To capture a fraction r of the data with a cube centered at the query, the cube's side must be r^{1/n}. The reason: a cube with side s has volume sⁿ, and for uniform data the fraction of points inside equals the volume. Setting sⁿ = r gives s = r^{1/n}. In 2 dimensions, a square holding 1% of the data has side √0.01 = 0.1. In 10 dimensions the same share needs 0.01^{0.1} = 0.63.

head: Dimension n
Side needed for 1% of the data
Side needed for 10%
table.caption: Side length (as a fraction of the range of each coordinate) of the cube holding a given share of uniform data: r^{1/n}.

body: In 10 dimensions a neighborhood containing only 1% of the data spans 63% of the range of every variable. It is not local at all.

For random points in high dimensions, the ratio of the farthest to the nearest distance from a query tends to 1: all points are almost equally far. Nearest and farthest neighbors become indistinguishable, and the neighbor voting becomes unreliable.

Covering each axis with 10 sample points takes 10ⁿ points in n dimensions. Real data usually lie near a lower-dimensional surface (an image of a face has far fewer degrees of freedom than pixels), which is why nearest neighbors can still work on real high-dimensional data, but only if the metric reflects that structure.

body.key: Remedies: reduce the dimension first (PCA or a learned embedding), select only relevant features, learn a metric, or use a model that makes assumptions (such as linearity) so that it does not depend on local data.

check.q: In 100 dimensions, a cube holding 1% of uniform data has side about
check.a: 0.955 of the range of each coordinate

sections.title: Kernel regression and fast search
body: A hard cutoff at k neighbors makes ŷ jump as the query moves. **Kernel regression** (the Nadaraya–Watson estimator) replaces it with a smooth weighting of all points by a kernel of the distance:

The bandwidth h plays the role of k: small h tracks the data closely, and large h averages broadly. It is a weighted average with weights that sum to one. (Locally weighted regression in the Linear Regression chapter fits a line instead of a constant at each query.)

example.title: Kernel regression at a query
example.problem: Data (x, y): (0, 2), (1, 4), (3, 10). Estimate y at x = 1.5 with a Gaussian kernel of bandwidth h = 1.
solution: The distances are 1.5, 0.5 and 1.5, so the weights are exp(−1.125) = 0.3247, exp(−0.125) = 0.8825 and exp(−1.125) = 0.3247. Their sum is 1.5319.
The estimate lies between the observed values and is closest to the nearest point's label, 4.

body: The same idea applied to the data points themselves, with the average taken over the kernel values, estimates a probability density. This is **kernel density estimation**: p̂(x) = (1/m) Σ K_h(x − x^{(i)}) with the kernel normalized to integrate to one.
Brute-force search costs O(mn) per query. Alternatives:

list: **k-d trees** and **ball trees** split space recursively and prune branches that cannot contain a nearer point. They give roughly O(log m) queries in low dimension (n below about 20) but degrade to brute force in high dimension.

**Approximate nearest neighbor** methods trade a small chance of missing the true neighbors for large speedups: locality-sensitive hashing (similar points collide in hash buckets), graph-based indexes (HNSW) and product quantization. These power vector search over billions of embeddings.
Reduce m by keeping only prototypes or condensing the training set.

check.q: In Nadaraya–Watson regression, the prediction is
check.a: a weighted average of the training labels, with weights from the kernel
wrong: the label of the single nearest point
a straight line fit to all points
the median label

quiz.q: Training data (x, y): (1, 2), (2, 4), (4, 9), (7, 13). A 2-nearest-neighbor regression predicts y at x = 3 as
quiz.why: The two nearest points are x = 2 and x = 4, both at distance 1, so the prediction is (4 + 9)/2 = 6.5. Using k = 3 would add x = 1 and give 5, and averaging all four labels gives 7.

quiz.q: On a line, the labels are 0 (A), 1 (A), 2.5 (B), 3 (B), 4 (A). For the query 2.2, the predictions for k = 1, 3 and 5 are
wrong: B, A, A
A, B, B
B, B, B
quiz.why: Sorted by distance the labels are B (2.5), B (3), A (1), A (4), A (0). The first neighbor is B, the first three are B, B, A, and all five are 3 A against 2 B.

quiz.q: What does a k-nearest-neighbor classifier predict when k equals the number of training points m?
quiz.a: The majority class of the whole training set, for every query
wrong: The label of the single nearest point
The Bayes optimal class at each query
A different class for every query, which gives zero training error
quiz.why: With k = m every query uses all the data, so the boundary has smoothed out completely. Zero training error is the property of k = 1.

quiz.q: A query has two neighbors: one at distance 1 with label 10, and one at distance 2 with label 20. With weights proportional to 1/distance, the regression prediction is about
quiz.why: The weights are 1 and 0.5, so the prediction is (1·10 + 0.5·20)/1.5 = 13.3. The unweighted average is 15, and reversing the weights gives 16.7.

quiz.q: A nearest-neighbor model uses 5 informative features. Fifty random, irrelevant features are added. What is the likely effect?
quiz.a: Accuracy drops, since the irrelevant features add noise to every distance
wrong: Accuracy is unchanged, since the informative features still count
Accuracy improves, since there are more features to separate the classes
Only the training time is affected, because the neighbors stay the same
quiz.why: The distance sums over all features, so random coordinates swamp the informative ones and the nearest neighbors become arbitrary.

quiz.q: Feature A takes values in [0, 1] and feature B in [0, 1000]. With Euclidean distance and no scaling, the neighbors are decided
wrong: almost entirely by feature A, since it is more precise
equally by the two, since distance is unit-free
by whichever feature has the lower variance
quiz.why: Differences in B are hundreds of times larger than in A, so they dominate the sum of squares. Standardizing the features removes the problem.

quiz.q: The Manhattan (L1) distance between (1, 2) and (4, 6) is
quiz.why: L1 distance is |1 − 4| + |2 − 6| = 3 + 4 = 7. The value 5 is the Euclidean distance.

quiz.q: Which pair of vectors has cosine similarity exactly 1?
quiz.why: Cosine similarity compares only direction. (3, 6) = 3·(1, 2), so the angle is zero. The pair (1, 2) and (−1, −2) has similarity −1.

quiz.q: At a point x, P(y = 1 | x) = 0.8. The asymptotic error of the 1-nearest-neighbor rule at that point is
quiz.why: The query and its neighbor have labels drawn independently from the same distribution, so they disagree with probability 2(0.8)(0.2) = 0.32. The Bayes rule errs only 0.20 of the time.

quiz.q: Which claim about the 1-nearest-neighbor rule is false?
quiz.a: As m → ∞, its error converges to the Bayes error for any distribution
wrong: Its asymptotic error is at most 2R*(1 − R*)
Its training error is zero when there are no conflicting duplicate points
Its decision regions are the cells of a Voronoi diagram
quiz.why: The Cover–Hart bound allows up to twice the Bayes error, and it is reached on some distributions. Consistency needs k → ∞ with k/m → 0.

quiz.q: Which choice of k as a function of the number of training points m makes k-NN consistent?
wrong: k = 5, whatever m is
k = m/2
quiz.why: Consistency requires k → ∞ but k/m → 0, so that neighborhoods contain many points yet shrink. A fixed k does not average enough, and k = m/2 is not local.

quiz.q: Data are uniform in the unit cube [0, 1]³. A cube centered at the query that holds 12.5% of the data has side
quiz.why: The fraction of data inside equals the volume s³, so s = 0.125^{1/3} = 0.5. Using the fraction itself, 0.125, ignores the dimension.

quiz.q: For random points in a very high-dimensional space, the ratio of the farthest distance to the nearest distance from a query
quiz.a: approaches 1, so neighbors become hard to distinguish from other points
wrong: grows without bound, so the nearest neighbor is ever more distinctive
approaches 0, so all the points collapse onto the query
stays equal to the ratio in two dimensions
quiz.why: Distances concentrate: all points are almost equally far from the query. A vote among the nearest few then carries little information.

quiz.q: To cover each coordinate axis with 10 sample points in a 6-dimensional space, how many points are needed?
quiz.why: A grid with 10 values per axis has 10ⁿ cells, which is 10⁶ for n = 6. The requirement grows exponentially with the dimension.

quiz.q: Nadaraya–Watson regression at a query has kernel values (2, 1, 1) for training labels (3, 6, 10). The estimate is
quiz.why: It is the kernel-weighted average Σ K y/Σ K = (6 + 6 + 10)/4 = 5.5. Dividing by the number of points gives 7.33, and skipping the division gives 22.

quiz.q: In kernel regression, what happens as the bandwidth h grows very large?
quiz.a: The prediction approaches the average of all training labels
wrong: The prediction approaches the label of the nearest training point
The prediction approaches a straight line through the data
The prediction becomes undefined, since the weights sum to more than one
quiz.why: With a very wide kernel all weights become nearly equal, giving the global mean. A tiny h makes the nearest point dominate. The weights are normalized to sum to one.

quiz.q: How do k-d trees perform for nearest-neighbor search as the dimension grows?
quiz.a: They give roughly O(log m) queries in low dimension but degrade toward brute force above about 20 dimensions
wrong: They give O(log m) queries in any dimension
They get faster as the dimension grows, since there are more splits
They are exact in low dimension and approximate in high dimension, with the same speed
quiz.why: In high dimensions the distances concentrate, so little can be pruned and the search must visit most of the points, which is the cost of brute force.

summary: k-NN predicts by majority vote (classification) or average (regression) of the k closest training points. There is no training, but each query scans the data. 1-NN gives Voronoi cells.
k controls complexity: small k has low bias and high variance. Choose it by cross-validation. Scale the features, since the metric defines similarity.
Cover–Hart: asymptotically, R* ≤ R_1NN ≤ 2R*(1 − R*). With k → ∞ slowly, k-NN is consistent.
The curse of dimensionality makes neighborhoods non-local and distances similar. Reduce dimension or learn a metric.
Kernel regression is a smooth weighted average of labels; the bandwidth plays the role of k. Search is accelerated with trees or approximate methods.

problems.q: Training points: class A at (0, 0), (1, 0); class B at (3, 3), (4, 3), (4, 4). Classify (2, 1) with k = 3.

Features: age (range 20–70) and income (range 20,000–120,000). Two people differ by 10 years and by 5,000 in income. Compare each difference's contribution to the squared distance before and after scaling each feature to the range [0, 1].
problems.solution: Before: age 10² = 100, income 5000² = 25,000,000, so income dominates by a factor of 250,000. After scaling: age 10/50 = 0.2 → 0.04; income 5000/100,000 = 0.05 → 0.0025. Age now contributes more.
problems.a: Unscaled income dominates by 250,000×; scaled, age contributes 0.04 and income 0.0025.

problems.q: A 1-NN classifier has asymptotic error 0.32. What is the largest the Bayes error R* could be, and the smallest?
What side length of the cube is needed to hold 5% of uniform data in 20 dimensions?
problems.a: About 0.86 of the range of each variable.

problems.q: Data (0, 1), (2, 5). Estimate y at x = 1 with kernel regression and any symmetric kernel.
problems.solution: x = 1 is equidistant from both points, so the weights are equal and ŷ = (1 + 5)/2 = 3.
